section.title: The Bride's Longing
section.sectionRationale: The Song opens by naming itself the Song of Songs, the best of songs, and plunges straight into the voice of a woman longing for her beloved. The movement runs from her opening cry for his kisses, through a candid confession that she feels weathered and unworthy, to a mounting exchange of praise between the lovers, and it closes with the first sounding of the refrain that will guard the whole book: do not awaken love until the time is right.
section.thesis: Love that is delighted in, spoken openly, and rightly ordered is a good gift of God; the bride longs for her beloved, finds herself desired in return, and learns that such love is to be awakened in its proper time.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the bride's opening longing and her confession that she is dark yet lovely; the growing exchange of praise between the bride, the bridegroom, and the friends; and the bride at rest in his embrace, sounding the refrain, do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.

units.label: Longing and the dark yet lovely bride

verses.text: This is Solomon’s Song of Songs.
Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your {{ahavah|love}} is more delightful than wine.
The fragrance of your perfume is pleasing; your name is like perfume poured out. No wonder the maidens adore you.
Take me away with you, let us hurry! May the king bring me to his chambers. We will rejoice and delight in you; we will praise your love more than wine. It is only right that they adore you.
I am dark, yet lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.
Do not stare because I am dark, for the sun has gazed upon me. My mother’s sons were angry with me; they made me a keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have neglected.
Tell me, O one I love, where do you pasture your sheep? Where do you rest them at midday? Why should I be like a veiled woman beside the flocks of your companions?
If you do not know, O fairest of women, follow the tracks of the flock, and graze your young goats near the tents of the shepherds.
I compare you, my {{raya|darling}}, to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots.
Your cheeks are beautiful with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels.
We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with beads of silver.
While the king was at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance.
My {{dodi|beloved}} is to me a sachet of myrrh resting between my breasts.
My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi.
How beautiful you are, my darling! Oh, how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves.
How handsome you are, my beloved! Oh, how delightful! The soft grass is our bed.
The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are fragrant firs.

units.label: At rest, and the refrain
units.note: do not awaken love too soon

verses.text: I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valley.
Like a lily among the thorns is my darling among the maidens.
Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest is my beloved among the young men. I delight to sit in his shade, and his fruit is sweet to my taste.
He has brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me is love.
Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love.
His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me.
O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken {{ahavah|love}} until the time is right.

ahavah.gloss: Love. The same word Scripture uses for love of God and neighbor. In the Song it is delighted, exclusive love between the man and the woman, more delightful than wine, and by 8:6 it is declared as strong as death.

raya.gloss: My darling, literally my companion or dear friend, the bridegroom’s recurring name for the bride. It joins tender affection to genuine friendship: love that is also companionship.

dodi.gloss: Beloved, the bride’s characteristic name for her man, my beloved, dodi. The root dod carries the sense of love and the loved one; it recurs like a refrain and expresses glad, exclusive belonging.

basic.context: The book calls itself the Song of Songs, the finest of all songs, and opens with a woman longing aloud for the man she loves. She admits she feels weathered and overlooked, dark from working in the sun, yet she calls herself lovely. The lovers begin to praise each other openly, and she rests in his embrace. Three times in the book, and first here, she warns the young women not to stir up love before its proper time. The plain sense is the beauty and dignity of love between a man and a woman.
basic.hermeneutics: The big question every reader asks is what kind of book this is. Is it a celebration of married love, an allegory of God’s love for His people, or both? The wisest answer holds them together: it truly sings the goodness of covenant love between husband and wife, and because God designed marriage as a living picture of Christ and the church, that love points beyond itself. Read this way, the Song is neither crude nor merely spiritualized away.
basic.originalLanguages: Two pet names run through the Song like refrains. The woman calls the man dodi, my beloved; the man calls her raya, my darling, a word that also means my companion or friend. The love itself is ahavah, the ordinary Hebrew word for love, the same used for loving God and neighbor. Here it is more delightful than wine.
basic.typology: Marriage was made from the beginning as a sign, the two becoming one flesh, Genesis 2. Paul says that mystery refers to Christ and the church, Ephesians 5. So the longing, the delight, and the belonging of these lovers picture, without being reduced to, the greater love of Christ for His people.
basic.christ: The bride’s cry, let him kiss me, her sense of being unworthy yet loved, and her rest under his banner of love, all echo the gospel: Christ loves and welcomes a people who feel unlovely, and His banner over them is love. The best of songs finally sings of the best of loves, the Bridegroom who gave Himself for His bride.
basic.god: God is the giver of love and delight. He is not embarrassed by the joy of husband and wife; He wrote it into creation and preserved this song in Scripture. He also teaches love’s right ordering, that it be awakened in its proper time.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2:24 gives the one flesh union the Song celebrates. Ephesians 5:31 to 32 reveals marriage as a sign of Christ and the church. Proverbs 5:18 to 19 commends delight in one’s spouse.
basic.oneStory: The Song opens the door on a good gift often treated with suspicion: the love of a man and a woman. Held rightly, it honors that love and lets it point higher, to the God who is love and to Christ who loves His bride.

context.literary:
The Song has no plot in the usual sense, and it has no narrator. It is a sequence of lyrics in which a woman, a man and a chorus of 'daughters of Jerusalem' take turns. The BSB footnote on 1:1 notes that the speaker labels found in many Bibles are supplied by translators from the gender and number of the Hebrew words, so even the division of voices is part of the reading work.

This first movement opens with a title, 1:1, and then drops straight into longing. The woman's first words are a wish, 'Let him kiss me,' and in the middle of the verse she turns from speaking about him to speaking to him, 'your love,' a shift of person that makes the poem feel like speech overheard. The movement then widens into a dialogue. She admits her darkness and her neglected vineyard, 1:5-6, and asks where he pastures his flock, 1:7. He answers gently, 1:8, and the two trade compliments with images drawn from garden, stable, desert oasis and house, 1:9-17.

The movement is arranged around a motion toward rest. It starts with a cry to be taken away, 1:4, and ends with her lying under his arm, 2:6, in a house whose beams are cedar, 1:17, and at the end she addresses the chorus and gives the first of the Song's three identical charges, 2:7. That same charge returns at 3:5 and 8:4, and the repetition is how the poem marks its main divisions.

The images are intentionally strange to a modern ear. Doves' eyes, a mare among chariots, a sachet of myrrh, a rose of Sharon: they are not photographs but compliments, built from what the lovers prize. The poem asks to be read as the speech of delight, not as a description.
context.historical:
The title attributes the Song to Solomon, 1:1, and 1 Kings 4:32 says that his songs numbered a thousand and five. The Hebrew preposition in the title can mean by, for or about Solomon, so the title alone does not settle authorship. Many readers hold Solomonic authorship, and others see Solomon as the royal figure in the poem. Either way the poem is set in the world of Israel's monarchy, with its royal tables, chambers and perfumes.

The woman's comparison, 'like the tents of Kedar,' draws on the nomads descended from Ishmael's son Kedar, Genesis 25:13. Their tents were woven of dark goat hair, so the image is of a weathered, dark covering, set beside 'the curtains of Solomon,' the finest hangings of a palace. She is saying that she is both. Her dark skin, 1:6, comes from the sun, and the reason she worked in the sun is given: her brothers were angry with her and set her to keep the vineyards. The bride is from a family with its own demands on her, and she has paid for them with her own garden.

The luxuries in the lovers' words, oil, myrrh, henna blossom from En-gedi, a sachet worn between the breasts, spiced wine, belong to a trading economy that brought Arabian and Egyptian goods into Israel. A mare among Pharaoh's chariots is a compliment that depends on Solomon's chariot trade with Egypt. The poem places love inside real wealth, and still the lovers treasure each other more than any of these goods.

The 'daughters of Jerusalem' are the young women of the city who stand as listeners, a chorus that watches and is addressed, and who in the poem need to be taught love's proper pace.
context.canonical:
Several threads tie this opening to the rest of Scripture. The first is Genesis. Genesis 2:24-25 describes a man and woman who become one flesh and are 'not ashamed.' The Song's lovers are comfortable with delight and with their bodies in the same way, and the bride's self-conscious 'Do not stare,' 1:6, shows the shadow of what the fall did to shame. The Song is a poem of Eden regained in a small way.

The second thread is the prophets' habit of describing God's love for Israel as marriage. Isaiah says, 'as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you,' Isaiah 62:5. Hosea says, 'I will betroth you to Me forever,' Hosea 2:19. Jeremiah remembers 'your love as a bride,' Jeremiah 2:2. The Song uses the same language of love, not as a hidden code but as a plain poem that the prophets' picture presupposes. Marriage was a good enough thing for God to use it for Himself.

The third thread is the New Testament. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says that the mystery 'is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church,' Ephesians 5:31-32. John the Baptist calls himself the bridegroom's friend, John 3:29, and the Book of Revelation looks to 'the marriage of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:7.

Jewish and Christian readers have long read the Song this way. The Jewish tradition read the lovers as God and Israel, and a famous saying attributed to Rabbi Akiva treats the Song as the holy of holies among the writings. Christian interpreters from Origen onward read the bride as the church or the soul, and Bernard of Clairvaux preached many sermons on the Song. The best of these readings keep the plain sense and let it point upward.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wants the first hearers to see that love between a man and a woman is a good thing that deserves to be spoken, praised and enjoyed. The Song gives desire a home: it belongs in the speech of a woman and a man who belong to each other, and the delight in it is God-given.

The poet also means the hearers to learn something about how love is ordered. The bride is not ashamed to want, and she is not afraid to ask, and the Song lets her speak first and most. But the first section ends with a charge that desire must not be forced early, 2:7. The wisdom teacher in the poem is the woman herself, speaking to those who are young. The hearers are to see that real delight needs trust, belonging and time, and that the poem's frankness and its restraint come from the same understanding.

The poet means to restore dignity to a woman who thinks herself overlooked. She says she is dark and neglected, and the man's answer is that she is beautiful, 1:15. The song says that being loved does not wait for a person to be impressive.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The Song describes a courtship and a wedding poem. It is not a code of conduct, and its speeches are the speech of lovers, not instructions. Most of what is said, the kissing, the longing, the lingering in the arms, is celebrated, and Scripture treats it as good within the bond the poem assumes, the love of a man and a woman who belong to each other, 2:16.

The one place where the poem steps back and gives an instruction is the charge to the daughters of Jerusalem, 2:7: do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right. That is prescriptive, and it is a word of wisdom for those who are not yet married. The charge is not a general ban on love. It is a warning against forcing it too soon, and the BSB's 'until the time is right' translates the Hebrew idea of 'until it pleases' or 'until it desires.' Love has a season.

It is also worth noticing what the Song does not command. It does not set out how a couple should behave in private, and it does not make the poetic images, a mare among chariots or a lily among thorns, into a template. Application should follow the poem's point: speak of love warmly, receive it humbly, and let it grow in its own time within a covenant.

debates.question: Is the Song about human love, about God and His people, or both?

views.label: Human married love, literally
views.case: The poem reads like love poetry throughout, with its frank delight, its physical imagery and its human speakers. Many modern readers take it as a celebration of marriage and nothing more, and note that the text never mentions God by name in a way that points to a hidden meaning. They hold that the allegorical readings of earlier centuries often had to ignore the plain sense.

views.label: An allegory of God and His people
views.case: Jewish tradition read the lovers as the LORD and Israel, and the church fathers and medieval interpreters read them as Christ and the church or the soul. They point to the marriage language of the prophets, Hosea 2:19-20 and Isaiah 62:5, and to Ephesians 5:31-32.

views.label: Literal first, pointing to Christ and the church
views.case: This view keeps the plain sense, since Scripture treats marriage as good and the poem as real love poetry, and holds that because God designed marriage as a sign of Christ and the church, the poem's love finds its deepest meaning there. Many Reformed and evangelical readers follow this path.

debates.bearing: The third reading avoids both losing the poem's plain sense and forcing a meaning on every detail. It lets the poem be about love and lets the New Testament say what love is a sign of.

debates.question: Who is speaking at 1:8 and 1:11?

views.label: The man answers the woman
views.case: Verse 8 reads naturally as a reply to 1:7, with the man gently telling her to follow the flock. The 'we' of verse 11 would be the man speaking with his companions, promising ornaments of gold.

views.label: The chorus speaks
views.case: Some see verse 8 as the daughters of Jerusalem answering her question, and verse 11 as the chorus speaking. The 'we' in verse 11 fits a group.

debates.bearing: The text itself does not name speakers, so the difference does not change the main reading. In either case her question is answered and her worth is affirmed, and the tenderness of verse 9 is the man's own.

study.originalLanguages:
The title shir hashirim, 'Song of Songs,' uses a Hebrew pattern for the superlative: the noun is repeated in the plural and in the construct, as in 'holy of holies' and 'king of kings.' It means the finest of all songs, the one song among a thousand and five, as 1 Kings 4:32 counts them. The phrase after it, lishlomo, uses a preposition that can mean 'of,' 'by,' 'for' or 'about,' which is why people argue about authorship without disturbing the plain meaning.

The word the BSB renders 'love' in 1:2 and again in 1:4 is not the common ahavah. It is the plural noun dodim, from the same root as dod, the word for 'beloved' in 1:13. Dodim names the physical and emotional expressions of love, caresses and love-making, and the plural carries the sense of many acts of love. The woman says that his dodim are better than wine. The word for 'beloved' that she uses of him, dodi, comes from the same root, so her whole address to him is built on the one word. The reader hears her call him 'my loves' and 'my lover' in the same breath.

In 1:5 she says shechorah ani venavah, 'I am dark, and lovely.' The Hebrew has the plain conjunction, which can be read as 'and' or as 'but,' and the BSB's 'yet' is one fair choice. Either way, the poem puts darkness and loveliness in the same breath without the second cancelling the first. The next verse says that 'the sun has gazed upon me,' a vivid way of saying that the sun has looked hard at her. The line then plays on a word: 'my own vineyard I have neglected' uses the same noun, karem, as the 'vineyards' she keeps, and a vineyard is an image the Song uses again for the woman herself, 8:12.

In 1:9 the man says 'my darling,' raya, a feminine form of the word for friend or companion It is the word for a close companion, and the Song uses it again and again. He also compares her to susati, 'my mare,' among Pharaoh's chariots. The horse is a creature of beauty and power, and the compliment is bold.

At 2:7 the charge is 'Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.' The two verbs, ta'iru and te'orerru, are verbs of stirring someone from sleep. The final phrase is ad shetechpatz, which can be rendered 'until it pleases' or 'until it desires.' Love is treated almost like a sleeper who wakes when it wills, and the instruction is to let it do so and not shake it awake. The oath 'by the gazelles and does of the field' uses words, tzeva'ot and ayelot, that some interpreters hear as an echo of divine titles, though the text does not say so. At 2:4 'banner,' degel, is a military word for a standard, as in Numbers 2:2, here used of love's claim over her.

typology.fulfillment: The prophets already use marriage as a picture of God and His people, Isaiah 62:5 and Hosea 2:19-20. Paul says that the one-flesh union of Genesis 2:24 is 'about Christ and the church,' Ephesians 5:31-32, and Revelation looks to the marriage of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7. The Song's tenderness, desire and belonging are the best human picture of this. The escalation is that Christ's love is not only felt, it is costly: He 'gave Himself up for her,' Ephesians 5:25. The type falls short because human lovers are two sinners, while the Bridegroom is sinless and the Bride is made spotless by His own work.

typology.type: The bride who is dark yet lovely
typology.fulfillment: The bride's confession, 'I am dark, yet lovely,' 1:5, pictures a person who is at once weathered by the world and still loved. The New Testament says that the church is presented to Christ 'as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish,' Ephesians 5:27. The correspondence is of someone who feels unworthy being valued, and the escalation is that He is the one who makes her lovely. The type falls short because the bride in the poem is lovely already, while the church is made so.

A banner marked a person's place and allegiance in Israel's camp, Numbers 2:2. The bride says that the king's banner over her is love, and the picture is of belonging under a protecting flag. In Christ the believer is held by a love from which nothing can separate, Romans 8:35, and the believer's life is 'hidden with Christ in God,' Colossians 3:3. The type is not a prophecy, it is a picture of the security of being claimed, and the New Testament names whose claim it is.

study.christ:
The Song is not quoted in the New Testament, so its link to Christ is made through the Bible's wider marriage theme, and that route should be taken with care. The path begins in Genesis, where the first marriage is a one-flesh union, Genesis 2:24. It continues in the prophets, who speak of God as husband, Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19-20. And in the New Testament Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom, Matthew 9:15, John the Baptist says that 'The bride belongs to the bridegroom,' John 3:29, and Paul says that the husband's love for his wife is a sign of 'Christ and the church,' Ephesians 5:32. The Song is the Bible's longest poem about that love, so a reader who follows Paul will hear the Song with the bridegroom in view.

At the beginning of the poem the bride is longing and unsure. She cries 'Take me away with you,' 1:4, and she feels weathered and overlooked, 1:5-6. What she receives is a welcome that does not wait for her to become impressive: 'How beautiful you are, my darling,' 1:15. That is the shape of the gospel. Christ does not call a people who have made themselves ready. He calls them, loves them and presents them to Himself, Ephesians 5:26-27. The bride who says 'my own vineyard I have neglected' is a fair picture of any person who has given their care to everything except what matters most. The answer to neglected vineyards is not a lecture but a bridegroom.

The poem also gives a picture of rest. At the end of the movement she says, 'His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me,' 2:6, and his banner over her is love, 2:4. Jesus said, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28. The believer is held, and holding is not earned.

The love in the Song is also guarded. The repeated charge that love not be woken early teaches that love is not to be used. It points to a Christ whose love is patient and whose bride is not pressed into belonging but won.

The caution is that every detail of the poem need not be made a code for Christ's work. The pearls and perfumes are compliments. What carries over is the pattern of a love that speaks warmly, receives the unlovely and rests.
study.god:
The Song shows first that God is a giver. He is not named in the poem's speeches, but the whole poem is full of gifts: fruit, wine, shade, garden, the body, and the love of one person for another. The Bible's own commentary, in Proverbs 5:18-19, tells a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth, and the Song is the extended form of that counsel. This tells us that God is not embarrassed by desire. He made it, and He keeps it in Scripture. A doctrine of God that cannot enjoy the delight of husband and wife has misread the Creator.

It shows also that God is a God of order. The one charge the poem repeats is that love must not be roused before its time, 2:7. It is not a charge against love but for it, because it treats love as precious enough to protect. The God who made love also set its season. That shapes worship: the believer does not use God's gifts as an appetite, and does not despise them as a danger. The believer receives them as given.

God is the one who sees and values. The bride feels dark and overlooked and the man says she is beautiful. A reader may hear in this the doctrine that God's regard for a person is not set by that person's standing in the world. The prophets say of Israel that God remembered 'the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride,' Jeremiah 2:2, and the poem allows that picture to be felt before it is explained.

A tension the Song holds is between delight and restraint. A people who only hear the call to restraint may think God cold. A people who only hear the delight may think God a servant of their wants. The poem keeps both together, and so should a doctrine of God. He gives richly and He gives in order.

Finally, the Song reminds the church that God's love is a love of desire, not only duty. The Lord says, 'I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with loving devotion,' Jeremiah 31:3. For worship, that means that adoration can be warm. The believer's love for God is allowed to be glad, to long and to rest, as the bride's does.

crossReferences.note: The first marriage: a man is united to his wife, they become one flesh, and they are 'not ashamed.' The Song's delight is the same delight, spoken as poetry. The bride's 'Do not stare,' 1:6, shows what the fall did to shame, and the poem moves toward a love in which there is no need to hide.

The wisdom teacher tells a young man to rejoice in the wife of his youth and to be captivated by her love. The Song is the longer, richer form of that advice, and the two books together show that wisdom includes delighting in a spouse.

The third and last time the charge appears, 'Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.' It closes the movement that began at 2:7 and the one at 3:5, and it shows that the refrain is the Song's way of marking its sections and holding its theme steady.

The Song's high point: love is 'as strong as death' and mighty waters cannot quench it. The longing of 1:2 grows into this claim. By the end the bride's cry for a kiss has become a declaration about the unstoppable strength of covenant love.

God's own words to Israel: 'as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.' The prophet takes the picture of a wedding delight and attaches it to God, which gives a basis for hearing the Song's love as an image of divine love.

God says, 'I will betroth you to Me forever,' and joins righteousness, justice, loving devotion, compassion and faithfulness. The marriage promise here is cast as a covenant, and it shows what the Song's love looks like when God is the bridegroom.

God remembers Israel's early love, 'your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness.' The marriage language is used for relationship to God. It is a reminder that devotion is wanted and that its loss is felt.

Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says that the mystery 'is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church.' This is the clearest New Testament license for hearing the Song's love as a picture of Christ's love, and it still treats marriage itself as real.

John the Baptist says, 'The bride belongs to the bridegroom,' and describes himself as the friend who is overjoyed to hear the bridegroom's voice. The same bridal picture is applied directly to Jesus, so that Christ is the bridegroom whose voice the believer waits to hear.

'The marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready.' The Bible ends its story with a wedding. The bride's longing in the Song finds its final answer in this day when the groom and the bride are joined.

Solomon composed three thousand proverbs, 'and his songs numbered a thousand and five.' This is the historical anchor for the title in 1:1. It tells us that the Song of Songs is the chosen one of a very large body of songs, which is what the superlative title claims.

Kedar is a son of Ishmael, and the 'tents of Kedar' in 1:5 are the dark tents of his nomadic descendants. The reference locates the bride's comparison in a real people and a real landscape, and it shows that the poem is rooted in the world of the patriarchal families.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a wedding of a kind. God makes a man and a woman, brings them together, and they are one flesh and not ashamed, Genesis 2:24-25. The very next chapter is the fall, and shame, blame and strained desire come in, Genesis 3:7-16. The Song of Songs stands in the space between. It is not Eden, because the bride is weathered and the vineyards are neglected, and it is not simply the fall, because delight is real and spoken without fear. It is a gift of God's goodness that has survived into a broken world, and it is told with a poet's honesty.

That is why the Song has its place in the canon. It tells people who live after Genesis 3 that the longing for union with another person is not a mistake. It was made, and it can be received. It also gives the longing a form: the love that is spoken, the love that is exclusive, the love that waits for its season. The charge of 2:7 is the reminder that what God gives He gives in order.

The rest of the Bible then picks up the picture and carries it upward. God is Israel's husband in the prophets, and Israel's unfaithfulness is the broken marriage, Hosea 2:19-20, Jeremiah 2:2. Jesus comes as the bridegroom, Matthew 9:15, and Paul says that human marriage was a sign of Christ and the church from the start, Ephesians 5:32. The Bible ends with the wedding supper, Revelation 19:7, and with the holy city 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2.

The longing of 1:2, 'Let him kiss me,' therefore finds its fullest answer in the new creation. There the bride is not weathered and the vineyards are not neglected, because the Bridegroom has made her ready. The Song gives believers a way to read their own desire: what is good in human love is a taste of the greater love to come, and what is incomplete in it is a pointer to the love that completes.

For the reader today, this means that the Song gives permission to hope and to rest. A lonely person can learn from it that longing is not a failure. A married person can learn that delight in a spouse is holy. And everyone can hear in the bride's cry, 'Take me away with you,' the cry of the church, 'Come,' Revelation 22:17.

quiz.q: What does the title Song of Songs mean?

options.text: The best or finest of all songs, a Hebrew way of naming the highest of its kind.
options.note: Song of Songs is a superlative, like King of kings, marking it the greatest of songs.

options.text: A song made up of many smaller songs stitched together.
options.note: It does gather many poetic units, but the phrase itself means the finest song.

options.text: A song to be sung only by kings.
options.note: Solomon is named, but the title marks excellence, not a royal audience.

options.text: A song about singing.
options.note: The title is a superlative naming the song’s surpassing worth.

quiz.q: How does the bride describe herself in 1:5 to 6?

options.text: Dark from working in the sun, yet lovely, honest about her weariness but sure she is beautiful.
options.note: She holds together real hardship and true loveliness.

options.text: Beautiful and untroubled, with nothing to confess.
options.note: She does know she is lovely, but the claim that she has nothing to confess misses her open lament over her neglected vineyard.

options.text: Ashamed and unwilling to be seen at all.
options.note: She is genuinely self-conscious about being stared at, yet she is not unwilling to be seen; she still calls herself lovely and longs to be near her beloved.

options.text: Wealthy and idle, kept from all work.
options.note: The opposite: her brothers made her keep the vineyards under the sun.

quiz.q: What is the best way to read the Song as a whole?

options.text: As a real celebration of married love that, because marriage pictures Christ and the church, also points beyond itself.
options.note: The both reading honors the plain sense and lets it point higher.

options.text: Only as an allegory of God’s love, with no reference to human marriage.
options.note: It does picture God’s love, but not by emptying the plain celebration of married love.

options.text: Only as a romance, with no larger meaning in Scripture.
options.note: It truly celebrates married love, yet Scripture ties marriage to Christ and the church.

options.text: As a manual of rules for courtship.
options.note: It is poetry that sings of love, not a rulebook, though it does guard love’s right time.

quiz.q: What is the refrain first sounded in 2:7?

options.text: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.
options.note: This charge, repeated three times, guards love’s proper season.

options.text: A warning to keep love secret forever.
options.note: The refrain does guard love, but by its timing, not by secrecy; the lovers praise each other openly.

options.text: A command never to marry.
options.note: It rightly senses a call to restraint and patience, yet overstates it; the refrain delays love to its proper time, it does not forbid marriage.

options.text: A call to awaken love as quickly as possible.
options.note: It says the opposite: do not awaken love before its time.

quiz.q: How does the dark yet lovely bride point to the gospel?

options.text: She pictures the church, unlovely in herself yet beautiful in her Beloved, desired before she is worthy.
options.note: Christ loves and beautifies a bride who feels dark and overlooked.

options.text: She shows that only the outwardly beautiful are loved.
options.note: The point is the reverse: she is loved though she feels weathered and unworthy.

options.text: She teaches that we must make ourselves lovely before God will draw near.
options.note: The gospel runs the other way: He loves and makes lovely those who are not.

options.text: She has no connection to Christ and the church at all.
options.note: The Song truly celebrates human married love in its own right, but Scripture reads that love as a sign of Christ and His church, Ephesians 5, so it does point beyond itself.

questions: The bride longs openly for her beloved and is unafraid to say so. Where do you long for God, and would you dare to voice that desire as honestly?
She calls herself dark, yet lovely, holding weariness and beauty together. How does it steady you to know Christ calls His people lovely even when they feel worn and overlooked?
His banner over me is love, she says. What would change this week if you truly lived under the banner of Christ’s love rather than under fear or performance?
Three times the Song warns not to awaken love before its time. Where in your life do you need patience to let something good unfold in its proper season?
The Song treats the love of husband and wife as a good and holy gift. How can you honor that gift, whether in your own marriage, in singleness, or in how you speak of others’ marriages?

translationNotes.note: Song of Songs is a Hebrew superlative, the finest of songs, like Holy of Holies or King of kings.
Dark, yet lovely can also be rendered dark and lovely; either way it holds together honest hardship and true beauty.
Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right is a refrain repeated at 3:5 and 8:4, guarding the proper season of love.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Song of Solomon 1:1-2:7, chapters 1 and 2. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose within each verse; embedded speaker labels in the source, such as The Friends and The Bride, were treated as headings and not included in the verse text. none remain.
